To find the work of adhesion ($W_A$) and the spreading coefficient ($S$), we can use the Young-Dupré equations provided:

Given:
* Liquid surface tension, $\gamma_{LV} = 25.777 \text{ mN/m}$ (which is equivalent to $\text{mJ/m}^2$)
* Contact angle, $\theta = 24.370^\circ$

First, calculate the cosine of the contact angle:
$\cos(24.370^\circ) \approx 0.91089$

**1. Work of Adhesion ($W_A$)**
The work of adhesion is the work required to separate the liquid and the solid, leaving two bare surfaces. 
$W_A = \gamma_{LV} (1 + \cos\theta)$
$W_A = 25.777 \times (1 + 0.91089) = 25.777 \times 1.91089 \approx 49.257 \text{ mJ/m}^2$

**2. Spreading Coefficient ($S$)**
The spreading coefficient determines whether a liquid will spontaneously spread out to cover the solid as a thin film.
$S = \gamma_{LV} (\cos\theta - 1)$
$S = 25.777 \times (0.91089 - 1) = 25.777 \times (-0.08911) \approx -2.297 \text{ mJ/m}^2$

**3. Spontaneous Wetting**
Spontaneous wetting (or complete spreading) of a solid by a liquid occurs only when the spreading coefficient is positive or zero ($S \ge 0$), which translates to a contact angle of exactly $0^\circ$. Because our spreading coefficient is negative (and $\theta > 0^\circ$), the liquid forms a droplet on the surface with a finite contact angle rather than spreading indefinitely. Thus, spontaneous wetting does not occur.
